title: The same four bytes, read two ways

prereqs.why: The two answers for every group of four bytes are the little-endian and big-endian readings of the same memory.
Assembling an integer out of bytes is shifting each one into place and combining them.
The signed reading is two's complement, and the whole exercise needs a type of known width.

statement:
You are handed the raw bytes of memory and have to decode them yourself.

Input is `n`, a multiple of 4, then `n` byte values in **increasing address
order**, each written in decimal from 0 to 255. For each group of four
consecutive bytes, print both readings:

```
le 0x<8 hex digits> <unsigned decimal> <signed decimal>
be 0x<8 hex digits> <unsigned decimal> <signed decimal>
```

Hex is lowercase, zero-padded to exactly 8 digits. The signed value is the
two's-complement interpretation of the same 32 bits.

```
input:   4                output:  le 0x12345678 305419896 305419896
         120 86 52 18              be 0x78563412 2018915346 2018915346
```

The bytes `120 86 52 18` are `0x78 0x56 0x34 0x12`. Read least-significant-byte
first they are the number `0x12345678`; read most-significant-byte first they
are `0x78563412` - a completely different number, about six times larger, from
the identical four bytes. Neither has its top bit set, so the signed and
unsigned readings agree here; the second sample shows what happens when it is
set.

### The point of the problem

Four bytes in memory are just four bytes. Which number they *mean* depends on a
convention your program has to apply:

```
address:   1000   1001   1002   1003
bytes:     0x78   0x56   0x34   0x12

little-endian:  0x12345678      (lowest address holds the LEAST significant byte)
big-endian:     0x78563412      (lowest address holds the MOST significant byte)
```

x86 and ARM in normal use are little-endian. Network protocols are big-endian,
which is why they call it *network byte order* and why `htonl` exists. Get it
wrong when parsing a file format or a packet and you read plausible nonsense -
`0x12345678` becomes `0x78563412`, a number 6 times larger, with no error
anywhere.

### Build it with shifts, not with a cast

The decoding is explicit arithmetic:

```cpp
std::uint32_t le = b0 | (b1 << 8) | (b2 << 16) | (b3 << 24);
```

Resist the temptation to `reinterpret_cast` the byte array to a `std::uint32_t*`
and dereference it. That would give you the **host's** byte order - so the
answer would change depending on the machine running it - and it is undefined
behaviour besides. The shift version produces the same answer everywhere, which
is exactly why real protocol code is written this way. The solution goes
through both problems.

### Boundary cases

All zero bytes. All `255`, which is `0xffffffff` - the unsigned value
4294967295 and the signed value -1. A value with the top bit exactly set,
`0x80000000`, which is the most negative 32-bit integer. A palindromic group
where both readings agree. Several groups in one input, so the loop steps by
four correctly.

### Platform assumptions

A byte is 8 bits and `std::uint32_t` exists and is exactly 32 bits - both
guaranteed on every platform these problems run on. Signed integers are two's
complement, which C++20 guarantees. The decoding is done with shifts, so **the
answer does not depend on the host's byte order** - that is the point, and it is
why this problem can have one correct output at all.
hints: Use `std::uint32_t` from `<cstdint>` for the assembled value, and read each byte into an `unsigned int`. Do not read bytes into a `char`: `std::cin >> c` on a char reads one *character*, not a number, so `120` would become the digit '1'.
Little-endian: the first byte of the group is the least significant, so it is shifted by 0, the next by 8, the next by 16, the last by 24. Big-endian is the same four shifts in the opposite order.

For the hex output: `std::hex << std::setw(8) << std::setfill('0')` from `<iomanip>`. `setw` applies to the next item only, while `hex` and `setfill` are sticky - so switch back with `std::dec` and `std::setfill(' ')` before printing the decimals.
